content: Allicin is a potent compound with antibacterial and antifungal properties, derived from garlic. It is the primary chemical responsible for the characteristic pungent, burning flavor of fresh garlic. Notably, allicin does not exist in garlic in its natural, intact state. Instead, it is formed when garlic is chopped, crushed, or otherwise damaged, triggering the enzyme alliinase to act on the precursor compound alliin, converting it into allicin. Alliin itself is an amino acid that does not participate in protein synthesis. Allicin is chemically unstable and degrades gradually when left standing. It is also highly sensitive to heat and is rapidly destroyed during cooking. Despite its instability, allicin has demonstrated potential medicinal applications. It has been shown to aid in combating atherosclerosis, possesses the ability to dissolve fats, and exhibits some antioxidant properties.
